[[Manhattan]], New York | coordinates = {{Coord|40|48|36|N|73|57|00|W|type:landmark_region:US-NY|display=inline,title}} | built = 1913–1914 | architect = [[George Keister]] | architecture = [[Classical Revival]] | added = {{Start date and age|November 17, 1983}} | refnum = 83004059{{NRISref |refnum=83004059|2007a}} | designated_other2 = New York City Landmark | designated_other2_date = {{Start date and age|June 28, 1983}} | designated_other2_number = 1299, 1300 }} }} The '''Apollo Theater''' (formerly the '''Hurtig & Seamon's New Theatre'''; also '''Apollo Theatre''' or '''125th Street Apollo Theatre''') is a multi-use [[Theater (structure)|theater]] at 253 [[125th Street (Manhattan)|West 125th Street]] in the [[Harlem]] neighborhood of [[Upper Manhattan]] in [[New York City]]. It is a popular venue for [[African Americans|Black American]] performers and is the home of the TV show ''[[Showtime at the Apollo]]''. The theater, which has approximately 1,500 seats across three levels, was designed by [[George Keister]] with elements of the [[Classical Revival architecture|neoclassical style]]. The facade and interior of the theater are [[New York City designated landmark]]s and are listed on the [[National Register of Historic Places]]. The [[Nonprofit organization|nonprofit]] Apollo Theater Foundation (ATF) operates the theater and a recording studio at the Apollo Theater, as well as two smaller auditoriums at the [[Victoria Theater (Harlem)|Victoria Theater]]. The Apollo was developed by theatrical producers [[Jules Hurtig]] and Harry Seamon as a [[burlesque]] venue in 1913, and originally served only white patrons. In 1928, the [[Minsky's Burlesque|Minsky brothers]] leased the theater for their own burlesque shows. Sydney Cohen acquired the theater in 1934, and it became a venue for black performers. Frank Schiffman and his family operated the theater from 1935 to 1976. A group of black businessmen briefly operated the theater from 1978 to 1979, and former Manhattan borough president [[Percy Sutton]] bought it at an auction in 1981. The Apollo reopened in 1985 following a major refurbishment that saw the construction of new recording studios. In September 1991, the [[New York State Urban Development Corporation]] bought the Apollo and assigned its operation to the ATF. Further renovations took place in the mid-2000s, and an expansion of the theater commenced in the 2020s. Among the theater's longest-running events is Amateur Night at the Apollo, a weekly show where audiences judge the quality of novice performances. Many of the theater's most famous performers are inducted in the Apollo Legends Hall of Fame, and the theater has commissioned various works and hosted educational programs. Over the years, the theater has hosted many musical, dance, theatrical, and comedy acts, with several performers often featured on the same bill. In addition, the theater has hosted film screenings, recordings, and tapings, as well as non-performance events such as speeches, debates, and tributes. The Apollo has had a large impact on [[African-American culture]] and has been featured in multiple books and shows. ==Site== The Apollo Theater is located at 253 West [[125th Street (Manhattan)|125th Street]], between [[Adam Clayton Powell Jr. Boulevard]] (Seventh Avenue) and [[Frederick Douglass Boulevard]] (Eighth Avenue), in the [[Harlem]] neighborhood of [[Upper Manhattan]] in [[New York City]].{{cite landmarks |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=o8ym5NeiylkC&pg=PA522 522]}}{{cite aia5|pages=528–529}} The irregular [[land lot]] has frontage on both 125th Street to the south and 126th Street to the north. The site covers {{cvt|17,454|ft2|m2}}, with a [[frontage]] of {{cvt|50|ft}} on 125th Street and a depth of {{cvt|200|ft|0}}.{{cite web |title=253 West 125 Street, 10027 |url=https://zola.planning.nyc.gov/l/lot/1/1931/10 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928101154/https://zola.planning.nyc.gov/l/lot/1/1931/10 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |access-date=March 25, 2021 |publisher=[[New York City Department of City Planning]]}} The theater is adjacent to the [[Victoria Theater (Harlem)|Victoria Theater]] to the west. Several [[MTA Regional Bus Operations]] routes stop outside the theater, while the [[New York City Subway]]'s [[125th Street station (IND Eighth Avenue Line)|125th Street/St. Nicholas Avenue]] station, served by the {{NYCS trains|Eighth center}}, is located one block to the west.{{cite NYC bus map|M}} == Design == The theater was designed by [[George Keister]] with elements of the [[Classical revival architecture|neoclassical]] style.{{cite nycland |page=202}} It was one of several theaters that Keister designed in that style, along with the [[Belasco Theatre (Broadway)|Belasco Theatre]], [[Bronx Opera House]], [[Selwyn Theater]], and [[Earl Carroll Theatre]].{{harvnb|ps=.|Landmarks Preservation Commission|1983|pp=3–4}} === Facade === The theater's main facade is on the south, toward 125th Street, and is three stories high.{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|1983|p=8}}; {{harvnb|National Park Service|1983|ps=.|p=2}} The ground floor has been renovated several times and consists of a ticket office to the west and a storefront to the east.{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|1983|ps=.|p=8}} The modern design of the ground floor dates to a renovation completed in 2005.{{cite news |last=Coleman |first=Chrisena |date=December 15, 2005 |title=Showtime for Apollo Facade |pages=109 |work=New York Daily News |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/daily-news-showtime-for-apollo-facade/130647990/ |access-date=September 18, 2023 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928101603/https://www.newspapers.com/article/daily-news-showtime-for-apollo-facade/130647990/ |url-status=live}}{{cite news |last=Pogrebin |first=Robin |date=December 15, 2005 |title=At Historic Apollo Theater, Restored Facade Is the Star of the Day |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/12/15/arts/at-historic-apollo-theater-restored-facade-is-the-star-of-the-day.html |access-date=September 18, 2023 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928101608/https://www.nytimes.com/2005/12/15/arts/at-historic-apollo-theater-restored-facade-is-the-star-of-the-day.html |url-status=live}} The eastern side of the ground floor contains a glass-and-steel storefront, with monitors installed in place of the original display cases. The modern-day box office is a semicircular steel structure that protrudes outward. The second and third stories are made of white glazed terracotta, which dates from the theater's opening in 1914. A [[cornice]] with [[dentil]]s runs horizontally across the facade just below the second floor. The second- and third-story windows are arranged vertically into four [[Bay (architecture)|bays]]. The bays are separated by three fluted [[pilaster]]s topped by [[Capital (architecture)|capitals]] in the [[Ionic order]], and there is a paneled pilaster with [[Tuscan architecture|Tuscan]] capitals outside each of the outermost bays. The capitals of all five pilasters contain [[Anthemion|anthemia]]. Within each bay, the second and third floors each contain a square window and are separated by [[spandrel]] panels with shields and fluting. Above the third-story windows are spandrels with [[Greek fret]] designs, as well as a metal cornice with [[modillion]]s. A steel [[Marquee (structure)|marquee]] was added above the ground floor in the 1940s; it stretched half the width of the facade and bore the name "Apollo" on its two side elevations. The marquee displayed letters with the name of the entertainer who were performing that night. Jack Schiffman, the son of former theater owner Frank Schiffman, recalled that the marquee also displayed various additional signs or movie posters.{{harvnb|Schiffman|1971|ps=.|p=12}} A vertical sign with the name "Apollo" was erected near the western end of the facade in the 1940s. A modern marquee with [[Light-emitting diode|LEDs]], resembling the original marquee, was installed in 2005. At the same time, the original vertical sign was replaced with the current yellow-and-red blade sign. === Interior === The theater has an L-shaped plan, with a narrow lobby leading to the main entrance on 125th Street, as well as the auditorium at the rear on 126th Street.{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission Interior|1983|p=8}}; {{harvnb|National Park Service|1983|ps=.|p=2}} Although the interior underwent several modifications in the mid-20th century, many of the 1910s-era decorations remained intact in 1983.{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission Interior|1983|ps=.|p=8}} The theater's original decorative features were preserved during the mid-1980s renovation.{{cite news |last=Goodman |first=Barak |date=December 14, 1985 |title=Apollo Hall of Fame preserves yesterday |page=23 |work=New York Amsterdam News |id={{proQuest|226461497}}}} ==== Lobby ==== The main lobby is a long and narrow space; some observers, including Jack Schiffman, have likened it to a bowling alley.{{harvnb|Schiffman|1971|ps=.|p=14}} The space was modified significantly in the 1930s and again in the 1960s, and the lobby was enlarged in the late 1970s. Following another renovation in 2006, the [[Tree of Hope]], a stump that performers rubbed for good luck, was moved to the lobby. The lobby occupies the western half of the ground level frontage on 125th Street; the eastern half of the frontage houses a store.{{harvnb|National Park Service|1983|ps=.|p=2}} The original main lobby had a group of murals. By the early 1970s, the lobby had been redecorated with a montage of notable entertainers who appeared at the Apollo.{{cite news |last=Naanes |first=Marlene |date=February 6, 2009 |title=Behind the Apollo's magic |page=2 |work=AM New York |id={{ProQuest|578160602}}}} There was also a ticket office and box office on one wall of the lobby.{{harvnb|Schiffman|1971|ps=.|p=15}} The modern-day lobby has two staircases, which lead to the first and second balconies of the auditorium.{{cite news |last=Goldscheider |first=Eric |date=June 19, 2005 |title=On Amateur Night, the Spotlight Can Singe |page=M.13 |work=Boston Globe |id={{ProQuest|404963773}}}} The space is illuminated by four grand chandeliers. There is a gift shop near the entrance.{{cite web |date=June 2, 2023 |title=Visit the Apollo |url=https://www.apollotheater.org/visit/ |access-date=September 1, 2023 |website=Apollo Theater |archive-date=September 1, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230901010048/https://www.apollotheater.org/visit/ |url-status=live}} {{As of|2023}}, a cafe is planned to be built within the lobby; it is expected to open in 2025.{{cite web |date=June 12, 2023 |title=Apollo Theater CEO Jonelle Procope to leave the historic landmark on safe financial ground |url=https://apnews.com/article/apollo-theater-ceo-jonelle-procope-47e0901411a201824be60a305eb46d37 |access-date=September 1, 2023 |website=AP News |archive-date=September 1, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230901010043/https://apnews.com/article/apollo-theater-ceo-jonelle-procope-47e0901411a201824be60a305eb46d37 |url-status=live}}{{cite web |last=Mitchell |first=Jessi |date=June 6, 2023 |title=Apollo Theater appoints Michelle Ebanks as new president and CEO |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/apollo-theater-appoints-michelle-ebanks-as-new-president-and-ceo/ |access-date=September 18, 2023 |website=CBS New York |archive-date=August 24, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230824200908/https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/apollo-theater-appoints-michelle-ebanks-as-new-president-and-ceo/ |url-status=live}} ==== Auditorium ==== [[File:Apollo Theater from the stage.jpg|thumb|The auditorium as seen from the stage]]The auditorium is at the north end of the building and is rectangular in plan, with curved walls, a domed ceiling, and two balcony levels over the orchestra level.{{harvnb|National Park Service|1983|ps=.|p=3}} The Apollo Theater was cited as having 2,000 seats in the 1930s{{cite news |date=June 11, 1935 |title=Apartment Resold in Uptown Deal; Investor Acquires Building of 6 Stories Housing 80 Families at 4,411 Broadway. |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1935/06/11/archives/apartment-resold-in-uptown-deal-investor-acquires-building-of-6.html |access-date=September 1, 2023 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=September 1, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230901215202/https://www.nytimes.com/1935/06/11/archives/apartment-resold-in-uptown-deal-investor-acquires-building-of-6.html |url-status=live}}{{cite news |date=June 11, 1935 |title=Cooperage Firm Leases Washington St. Property |page=34 |work=New York Herald Tribune |issn=1941-0646 |id={{ProQuest|1221977933}}}} and 1,700 seats in the 1970s;{{cite magazine |last=Terry |first=Ken |date=March 6, 1985 |title=Music-Records: Apollo Theatre Set To Reopen In May With NBC-TV Special; Extensive Music Sked In Works |magazine=Variety |volume=318 |issue=6 |pages=369, 372 |id={{ProQuest|1438441439}}}} it was described in 1985 as having 1,500{{cite news |date=May 25, 1985 |title=Facts About Harlem Landmark And Restoration |page=2 |work=New Pittsburgh Courier |id={{ProQuest|201767452}}}} or 1,550 seats.{{cite news |last=Robertson |first=Nan |date=May 20, 1985 |title=Apollo Amateur Night Returning This Week |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1985/05/20/theater/apollo-amateur-night-returning-this-week.html |access-date=September 18, 2023 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928101918/https://www.nytimes.com/1985/05/20/theater/apollo-amateur-night-returning-this-week.html |url-status=live}} By the early 2010s, the theater had 1,536 seats.{{cite news |last=Miller |first=Tricia |date=April 22, 2010 |title=75 Years of the Real Thing: Apollo Theater Is Celebrated |work=Roll Call |id={{ProQuest|324361386}}}} The seats were refurbished in the 1980s and again in 2006, when wide cranberry-colored seats were installed. The bottom of each row of seats is illuminated by aisle lighting. In addition, there is a seating area for disabled patrons.{{cite news |last=Misani |first= |date=February 23, 2006 |title=The Apollo: "A Very Special Lady" once again is sitting pretty |page=19 |work=New York Amsterdam News |id={{proQuest|390363543}}}} On each level, the seats are divided by two central aisles.{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission Interior|1983|p=8}}; {{harvnb|National Park Service|1983|ps=.|p=3}} As part of a 2024 renovation, the Apollo Theater Foundation planned to add 29 seats on the orchestra level.{{cite web |last=Kvetenadze |first=Téa |date=June 18, 2024 |title=Details, renderings unveiled for major restoration of Apollo Theater in Harlem |url=https://www.nydailynews.com/2024/06/18/details-renderings-unveiled-for-major-restoration-of-iconic-apollo-theater-in-harlem/ |access-date=August 20, 2024 |website=New York Daily News}} The rear (western) end of the orchestra contains a standing rail with [[scagliola]]. Scagliola decorations, composed of scrolls supporting a triangular [[pediment]], are also placed around the doorways on the rear wall of the orchestra. Fluted columns on the orchestra level support the first balcony; the lower parts of the columns are devoid of ornamentation. The orchestra is [[Rake (theatre)|raked]], sloping down toward an [[orchestra pit]] in front of the stage. The front walls of the auditorium flank a flat [[proscenium]] opening in the center. The balconies are also raked and contain similar scagliola decorations to the orchestra level. The balconies' fronts have brass handrails and are decorated with plasterwork motifs. At the first balcony are square columns supporting the second balcony. The second balcony was described by author James V. Hatch as "the bird's nest", since audiences in the second balcony could see the entire theater.{{harvnb|Carlin|Conwill|2010|ps=.|p=59}} On either side of the proscenium are two boxes each on the first and second balcony levels, which are accessed by their own staircases and are housed within round-arched openings. The [[spandrel]]s above the arches contain classical motifs, and the boxes have varying amounts of decorations. The proscenium arch has a surround with [[colonnette]]s on either side of the arch and a molded band and entablature running atop it. The surround and entablature both contain decorative plaster motifs. Above the boxes and the proscenium arch is a cornice with large dentils, as well as a plaster [[frieze]] decorated with foliate motifs. The ceiling is slightly [[Coved ceiling|coved]] at its edge. At the center of the ceiling is a semicircular dome with a medallion surrounded by a molding of [[cornucopia]]. The theater was mechanically advanced for its time, with a ventilation system to remove cigarette smoke, as well as electric lights.{{cite magazine |date=January 11, 1913 |title=Burlesque News of the Week: Another Theater for Eastern Wheel |magazine=The Billboard |volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=8 |id={{ProQuest|1031441492}}}} The ventilation system was rebuilt when the theater was renovated in the 1980s, and lighting trusses were added at that time.{{cite magazine |last=Fadden |first=James |date=December 16, 1988 |title=N.Y.'s Apollo Theatre Combines History With Teleproduction |magazine=Back Stage |volume=29 |issue=51 |pages=1, 44 |id={{ProQuest|962754582}}}} ==== Other spaces ==== In addition to the main auditorium, the ground floor had a store to the east of the lobby. There originally was a cafe and cabaret in the basement, which served as a rehearsal space and was converted into a staff recreation room in the 1940s.{{cite news |date=August 18, 1945 |title=Apollo Gets Face Cleaned; To Open Friday, Aug. 24 |page=21 |work=New York Amsterdam News |id={{proQuest|225996878}}}} In addition, there were a ladies' parlor and men's smoking room, which were enlarged in the 1940s.{{cite news |last=DeLeighbur |first=Don |date=August 25, 1945 |title=Harlem's Apollo Being Renovated; Reopen With Russe, Brown Dots |page=13 |work=Philadelphia Tribune |id={{ProQuest|531759273}}}} The second story originally had a dining room, while the third story had meeting rooms and lofts. By the 1980s, the second and third floors were being used as storage space and offices, with small rooms on both stories. The third floor also has a [[sound stage]]; to accommodate this use, the windows on that story were covered up in 1985.{{cite news |last=Barker |first=Cyril Josh |date=February 7, 2008 |title=New changes at the Apollo |page=15 |work=New York Amsterdam News |id={{proQuest|2663431344}}}} When the Apollo Theater was developed, the dressing rooms were placed in a separate annex with showers and baths. The dressing rooms are simple in design. There is a wall of signatures in the dressing room. The Apollo's historian Billy Mitchell said in 2012, "Anyone who's been to or performed at the Apollo in the last 20 years has their name on the wall—from Pee-wee Herman to the president of the United States".{{cite news |last=Feuer |first=Alan |date=October 13, 2012 |title=At Home in the Apollo Theater |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/10/14/nyregion/billy-mitchell-at-home-in-the-apollo-on-sundays.html |access-date=September 18, 2023 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928101138/https://www.nytimes.com/2012/10/14/nyregion/billy-mitchell-at-home-in-the-apollo-on-sundays.html |url-status=live}} A production studio for TV broadcasts and video productions was constructed on top of an adjacent wing during the 1980s.{{cite news |last=Walker |first=Robin |date=September 27, 1987 |title=The Apollo Showbiz Anchor For 125th St. |page=7 |work=Newsday |issn=2574-5298 |id={{ProQuest|277829082}}}} The studio is variously cited as covering {{convert|3500|ft2}},{{cite news |date=January 10, 1989 |title=Stevie Wonder records at the Apollo Theatre Television Center |page=8C |work=Philadelphia Tribune |id={{ProQuest|532982612}}}} {{convert|3800|ft2}}, or {{convert|4000|ft2}}.{{cite news |date=May 11, 1991 |title=The World Famous Apollo Theatre: its history and its present needs |page=13 |work=New York Amsterdam News |id={{proQuest|226303343}}}} It could record 24 [[Track (music)|tracks]] at once and was equipped with 96 microphone lines connecting with the auditorium. The studio has been used by media companies such as advertising firm [[Saatchi & Saatchi]] and [[Black Entertainment Television]].{{cite news |last=Thomas |first=Don |date=September 20, 2000 |title=The Apollo Theater Hosts BET Fall 2000 Season with an Elaborate Inside – Out Taping and Lavish Block Party |page=27 |work=New York Beacon |id={{ProQuest|367896700}}}} ==History== In the late 19th century, Harlem was developed as a suburb of New York City and was inhabited largely by upper-middle-class whites.{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|1983|p=1}}; {{harvnb|National Park Service|1983|ps=.|p=4}} Black residents began moving to Harlem in the beginning of the 20th century with the development of row houses, apartments, and the [[Early history of the IRT subway|city's first subway line]].{{cite news |last=Josh |first=Getlin |date=July 9, 1999 |title=Column One; Corporate Show Time at the Apollo; as White Investment Capital Revives Harlem, the Nightspot That is Its Soul May Rise Again. But Doubts and Struggles Abound. |page=1 |work=Los Angeles Times |issn=0458-3035 |id={{ProQuest|421403373}}}} By the early 20th century the neighborhood had several [[vaudeville]], [[burlesque]], [[film]], and [[Legitimate theatre|legitimate]] theaters centered around 125th Street and [[Seventh Avenue (Manhattan)|Seventh Avenue]],{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|1983|ps=.|p=2}} which led to the corridor being known as "Harlem's 42nd Street".{{cite web |last=Morehouse |first=Ward III |date=August 10, 2001 |title=Harlem's Apollo plans brief intermission |url=https://www.csmonitor.com/2001/0810/p20s1-almp.html |access-date=September 18, 2023 |website=The Christian Science Monitor |issn=0882-7729 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928100554/https://www.csmonitor.com/2001/0810/p20s1-almp.html |url-status=live}} Among the operators of these early theaters were theatrical producers Jules Hurtig and Harry Seamon, who leased the Harlem Music Hall at 209 West 125th Street in 1897.{{cite book |last=Brown |first=T.A. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kvYZnk5lBWsC&pg=PA605 |title=A History of the New York Stage from the First Performance in 1732 to 1901 |publisher=Dodd, Mead |year=1903 |page=605 |issue=v. 3 |access-date=2023-09-29 |archive-date=2023-09-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928100907/https://books.google.com/books?id=kvYZnk5lBWsC&pg=PA605 |url-status=live}}{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|1983|ps=.|p=3}} Hurtig and Seamon produced several shows starring black superstars [[Bert Williams]] and [[George Walker (vaudeville)|George Walker]] between 1898 and 1905.''Introducing Bert Williams: Burnt Cork, Broadway and the story of America's first Black star.'' Camille F. Forbes. Basic Books. The Music Hall was converted to burlesque {{Circa}} 1911. === Burlesque theater === ==== Development and early years ==== C. J. Stumpf & H. J. Langhoff of [[Milwaukee]], Wisconsin,{{cite magazine |date=June 29, 1912 |title=Plans Filed for New Construction Work |url=https://rerecord.library.columbia.edu/document.php?vol=ldpd_7031148_049&page=ldpd_7031148_049_00001842 |magazine=The Real Estate Record: Real estate record and builders' guide |volume=89 |pages=1422 |via=[[Columbia University|columbia.edu]] |number=2311 |access-date=September 29, 2023 |archive-date=August 24, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230824200903/https://rerecord.library.columbia.edu/document.php?vol=ldpd_7031148_049&page=ldpd_7031148_049_00001842 |url-status=live}} acquired land on 125th and 126th Street from the Cromwell estate and Lit family around 1911 or 1912.{{cite news |date=June 21, 1912 |title=Lease Harlem Property for Theatre |pages=14 |work=New-York Tribune |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/new-york-tribune-lease-harlem-property-f/130578988/ |access-date=September 18, 2023 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928100554/https://www.newspapers.com/article/new-york-tribune-lease-harlem-property-f/130578988/ |url-status=live}} They announced plans in June 1912 for a three-story commercial structure at 253 to 259 West 125th Street, with a 2,500-seat burlesque theater in the rear, at 240 to 260 West 126th Street.{{cite news |date=June 23, 1912 |title=New Harlem Theatre; To be Built On West 125th Street |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1912/06/23/archives/new-harlem-theatre-to-be-built-on-west-125th-street-for-hurtig.html |access-date=September 18, 2023 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928095840/https://www.nytimes.com/1912/06/23/archives/new-harlem-theatre-to-be-built-on-west-125th-street-for-hurtig.html |url-status=live}} [[Jules Hurtig|Hurtig and Seamon]], who had been leasing the nearby Harlem Music Hall, wanted a larger venue to accommodate the burlesque productions of the [[Columbia Amusement Company]], which they had joined. They were set to lease the theater for 30 years for a total of $1.375 million; the theater itself would cost $200,000. Work could not begin until the existing leases on the site expired the following May. Stumpf and Langhoff hired Keister to design the theater, while either Cramp & Company{{cite magazine |date=July 20, 1912 |title=Current Building Operations |url=https://rerecord.library.columbia.edu/document.php?vol=ldpd_7031148_050&page=ldpd_7031148_050_00000182&no=5 |magazine=The Real Estate Record: Real estate record and builders' guide |volume=90 |pages=124 |via=[[Columbia University|columbia.edu]] |number=2314 |access-date=September 29, 2023 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928101903/https://rerecord.library.columbia.edu/document.php?vol=ldpd_7031148_050&page=ldpd_7031148_050_00000182&no=5 |url-status=live}} or the Security Construction Company was hired as the general contractor. [[Ralph Cooper]] was hired as the emcee the same year.{{cite news |date=August 6, 1992 |title=Ralph Cooper, Who Found Stars At Apollo's Amateur Nights, Dies |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1992/08/06/arts/ralph-cooper-who-found-stars-at-apollo-s-amateur-nights-dies.html |access-date=September 1, 2023 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=January 25, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200125175609/https://www.nytimes.com/1992/08/06/arts/ralph-cooper-who-found-stars-at-apollo-s-amateur-nights-dies.html |url-status=live}} After Cohen died in late 1935, the Opera House became a movie theater, while the Apollo continued to present stage shows.{{harvnb|Fletcher|2009|ps=.|pp=40–41}}{{harvnb|Schiffman|1971|ps=.|p=49}} The Apollo was rebranded as "The Only Stage Show in Harlem". Initially, the Apollo attracted [[blues]] and [[ragtime]] performers, as well as comedians and [[big band]]s.{{harvnb|Carlin|Conwill|2010|ps=.|p=143}} Early shows were accompanied by a [[chorus line]] of 16 girls, most of whom were fair-skinned;{{harvnb|Carlin|Conwill|2010|ps=.|p=124}} the chorus girls were no longer employed at the theater by the late 1930s.{{cite news |last=Day |first=Sherri |date=November 26, 2000 |title=City Lore; Chorus Girls of Harlem Challenge Father Time |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/11/26/nyregion/city-lore-chorus-girls-of-harlem-challenge-father-time.html |access-date=September 18, 2023 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928101737/https://www.nytimes.com/2000/11/26/nyregion/city-lore-chorus-girls-of-harlem-challenge-father-time.html |url-status=live}}{{harvnb|Carlin|Conwill|2010|ps=.|p=127}} The ''[[New York Amsterdam News]]'' described the Apollo in 1939 as "the only theatre in the country where Negro performers are predominantly featured", at a time when many other venues still did not allow black performers.{{cite news |date=August 5, 1939 |title=Frank Schiffman: Pro and Con His Apollo Theatre Stands as a Bulwark Between Performers and Crackup of Local Showlife Records "Some Other Spring" |page=17 |work=New York Amsterdam News |id={{proQuest|226123934}}}} The Apollo temporarily closed in mid-1940 for upgrades,{{cite news |last=Burley |first=Dan |date=July 27, 1940 |title=Apollo Theatre Closes Down: Showfolk Left in Pretty Pickle as Schiffman Decides To Transfer Streamlined Shows to Harlem Opera House |page=21 |work=New York Amsterdam News |id={{proQuest|226213640}}}}{{cite news |last=Rowe |first=Billy |date=July 27, 1940 |title=Vaudeville at the Apollo Ends This Week: House Closing to Check Trend; Plan New Entertainment |page=20 |work=Pittsburgh Courier |id={{ProQuest|202082311}}}} reopening that September.{{cite news |last=Smith |first=Isadora |date=September 7, 1940 |title=Apollo Theatre Reopens: New Glamour and Glitter Adds Another Page to Harlem's Joy Reopening of Apollo Theater Glamorized in Harlem |page=21 |work=Pittsburgh Courier |id={{ProQuest|202063791}}}} The theater began showing musical comedies for the first time in February 1941.{{cite news |last=Smith |first=Isadora |date=February 8, 1941 |title=Harlem First Nighters Set For "Tan Manhattan": Flournoy Miller and Nina Mae McKinney to Head Big Revue At Apollo—Show Being Readied For "Kleigh Lights" Premiere |page=20 |work=Pittsburgh Courier |id={{ProQuest|202095038}}}}{{cite news |last=Burley |first=Dan |date=February 22, 1941 |title=Up Harlem Way Comes to Apollo: New Entertainment Policy at 125th St. House Based on Campaign We Waged Last Summer for Better Entertainment Values for Harlemites |page=20 |work=New York Amsterdam News |id={{proQuest|226129389}}}} Jazz performances and bebop at the Apollo were popular in the 1940s, and [[Gospel music|gospel]] was hosted sporadically.{{harvnb|Carlin|Conwill|2010|ps=.|pp=158–159}} The Apollo appealed to mixed-race audiences in the 1940s; on Sundays, as much as four-fifths of the audience were white.{{harvnb|Schiffman|1971|ps=.|pp=49–50}} During World War II, the theater offered 35 free tickets to members of the U.S. armed forces, and entertainers at the Apollo performed at the nearby Harlem Defense Recreation Center on Tuesday nights.{{cite news |date=July 25, 1942 |title=Service Men Sorry Apollo Theatre Is Closed for Summer |pages=10 |work=The New York Age |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-new-york-age-service-men-sorry-apoll/131056378/ |access-date=September 1, 2023 |archive-date=September 1, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230901225942/https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-new-york-age-service-men-sorry-apoll/131056378/ |url-status=live}} Schiffman closed the theater temporarily for renovations in August 1945. The project cost $45,000 and entailed new sound systems, a remodeled orchestra pit, women's and men's lounges, a staff recreation room, and modifications to decorations. After World War II, the theater occasionally staged a chorus line with six acts. By 1946, Schiffman had announced plans to widen the theater and add an air-cooling system when construction materials became available.{{cite news |date=May 11, 1946 |title=Schiffman Scouts Charge Apollo Needs Overhauling |page=25 |work=New York Amsterdam News |id={{proQuest|225988270}}}} The theater was sold in 1949 to the Harlem Apollo Realty Corporation, although Schiffman and Brecher continued to operate the Apollo.{{cite news |date=January 22, 1949 |title='Historic' Apollo Changes Hands in Sale: Theatre, Harlem Tradition |page=14 |work=New York Amsterdam News |id={{proQuest|531825272}}}} That year, they began experimenting with staging [[Broadway theatre|Broadway]]-class shows at the Apollo.{{cite news |date=March 26, 1949 |title=Legit Theatre Slated To Take Over W. 125th Street: "Anna Lucasta" Set For Apollo To Drop Stage Show And Movie For Full-fledged Drama Trial |page=24 |work=New York Amsterdam News |id={{proQuest|225957784}}}}{{cite news |date=April 5, 1949 |title=Anna Lucasta opens Al Apollo Theatre |page=12 |work=Philadelphia Tribune |id={{ProQuest|531822264}}}} Schiffman's sons Jack and Robert began working at the theater in the late 1940s and early 1950s. ==== 1950s and 1960s ==== As the years progressed, variety shows were presented less often. The Apollo started staging rock music concerts when that genre became popular, and the big bands gave way to [[Rhythm and blues|R&B]] performances.{{harvnb|Carlin|Conwill|2010|ps=.|p=145}}{{harvnb|Carlin|Conwill|2010|ps=.|p=149}} The theater also began hosting different musical genres such as [[Mambo (music)|mambo]] and gospel.{{cite news |date=January 19, 1956 |title=Theatres Generates Interest Following Apollo Gospel Show |page=2 |work=Atlanta Daily World |id={{ProQuest|491076128}}}}{{harvnb|Carlin|Conwill|2010|ps=.|pp=160–161}} There were often two shows a day if a headliner was performing, and it showed movies at other times. Additionally, the theater was closed for upgrades for two weeks every August;{{cite news |date=August 5, 1961 |title=Apollo Shuts For Annual Clean-Up Time |page=17 |work=New York Amsterdam News |id={{proQuest|225429617}}}} a large [[CinemaScope]] screen was installed during one such closure in 1955.{{cite news |date=August 6, 1955 |title=Apollo Adding 'CinemaScope' During Closing |pages=9 |work=The New York Age |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-new-york-age-apollo-adding-cinemasc/131403657/ |access-date=September 7, 2023 |archive-date=September 7, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230907211304/https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-new-york-age-apollo-adding-cinemasc/131403657/ |url-status=live}} In 1957, [[Buddy Holly and the Crickets]] became the first white act to perform at the theater since it became centered on providing African American entertainment.{{cite news|url=https://www.thevintagenews.com/2018/08/30/buddy-holly-apollo-theatre/|title=Buddy Holly was the First White Act to Play the Apollo Theater in Harlem|first=Marea|last=Harris|publisher=The Vintage News|date=August 30, 2018|access-date=June 6, 2025}} By the late 1950s, [[Variety (magazine)|''Variety'']] magazine criticized the theater for "allowing some of its actors to carry on with assorted vulgarisms".{{cite news |date=March 30, 1957 |title=Variety magazine blasts Harlem's Apollo Theatre |page=10 |work=Afro-American |id={{ProQuest|491076128}}}} A typical booking consisted of five or six performances per day for seven days. The Apollo was one of the few remaining venues for black entertainers in Harlem during that time, although other venues such as the [[Waldorf Astoria New York]] and [[Copacabana (nightclub)|Copacabana]] had started allowing black performers.{{cite magazine |last=Cohen |first=Joe |date=January 4, 1956 |title=Vaudeville: Show Biz Long Proved There's No Frontier On Talent; Negro Artists' Great Progress' |magazine=Variety |volume=201 |issue=5 |page=414 |id={{ProQuest|1017015390}}}} Even so, many popular black artists such as [[Eartha Kitt]] and [[Sammy Davis Jr.]] regularly returned for "the folks who can't make it downtown".{{cite news |date=February 8, 1964 |title=Harlem's Heart Beats Message on 125th St.; Tells of Hope, Anger and Frustration of Negro Race |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/02/08/archives/harlems-heart-beats-message-on-125th-st-tells-of-hopeanger-and.html |access-date=September 7, 2023 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=September 7, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230907211305/https://www.nytimes.com/1964/02/08/archives/harlems-heart-beats-message-on-125th-st-tells-of-hopeanger-and.html |url-status=live}} Robert Schiffman took over the theater's management in 1960{{cite web | last=Hinckley | first=David | title=Harlem's legendary Apollo Theater celebrates its 80th anniversary | website=New York Daily News | date=January 12, 2014 | url=https://www.nydailynews.com/2014/01/12/harlems-legendary-apollo-theater-celebrates-its-80th-anniversary/ | access-date=December 2, 2023}} or 1961. He kept prices low to cater to the local community, and he tried to attract up-and-coming talent by talking with local DJs and listening to music at nearby bars.{{cite news|last=Williams|first=Alex|date=2023-09-15|title=Bobby Schiffman, Guiding Force of the Apollo Theater, Dies at 94|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/09/15/arts/music/bobby-schiffman-dead.html|access-date=2023-12-02|issn=0362-4331}} The 1960s saw the rising popularity of R&B at the Apollo, as well as mixed-genre productions.{{harvnb|Carlin|Conwill|2010|ps=.|p=197}} The theater was renovated slightly in 1960,{{cite news |date=August 17, 1960 |title=Apollo Will Reopen Friday |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1960/08/17/archives/apollo-will-reopen-friday.html |access-date=September 7, 2023 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=September 7, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230907195739/https://www.nytimes.com/1960/08/17/archives/apollo-will-reopen-friday.html |url-status=live}} and new sound-amplification equipment and lighting was added in August 1961. During the 1964 Harlem riots, the Apollo temporarily screened movies exclusively due to decreased patronage.{{cite news |date=August 1, 1964 |title=Harlem unrest has famed Apollo Theatre in middle |page=11 |work=Afro-American |id={{ProQuest|532170449}}}}{{cite magazine |date=July 22, 1964 |title=Apollo Theatre Owner Ponders on Calm Before Another Harlem Storm? |magazine=Variety |volume=235 |issue=9 |pages=1, 78 |id={{ProQuest|1014824591}}}} The lobby and auditorium were renovated in 1967;{{cite news |date=August 12, 1967 |title=Apollo Theater To Reopen Next Week |page=19 |work=New York Amsterdam News |id={{proQuest|226809516}}}} the project was conducted almost entirely by black workers and cost $50,000.{{cite news |date=August 26, 1967 |title=Black Workers Give Theatre A New Look |page=1 |work=New York Amsterdam News |id={{proQuest|226720589}}}}{{cite news |date=September 16, 1967 |title=Apollo renovation was a black affair |page=11 |work=Afro-American |id={{ProQuest|532192871}}}} Business began to decline after the [[Civil Rights Act of 1964]] was passed, allowing black entertainers to perform in nightclubs and hotels.{{cite news |last=Shipp |first=E. R. |date=May 31, 1991 |title=Harlem's Apollo Fights to Keep the Lights On |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1991/05/31/nyregion/harlem-s-apollo-fights-to-keep-the-lights-on.html |access-date=September 18, 2023 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928102157/https://www.nytimes.com/1991/05/31/nyregion/harlem-s-apollo-fights-to-keep-the-lights-on.html |url-status=live}}{{cite magazine |last=Carter |first=Chelsea J. |date=November 30, 1998 |title=Show Goes on at the Apollo Theatre |magazine=Network Journal |volume=6 |issue=2 |page=5 |id={{ProQuest|222637371}}}} The Apollo was smaller than similar venues; the neighborhood's economy was in decline; and the Apollo was not near other popular venues.{{cite news |last=Fraser |first=C. Gerald |date=April 15, 1975 |title=Apollo Finds It Hard for the Show to Go On |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1975/04/15/archives/apollo-finds-it-hard-for-the-show-to-go-on.html |access-date=September 18, 2023 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928100546/https://www.nytimes.com/1975/04/15/archives/apollo-finds-it-hard-for-the-show-to-go-on.html |url-status=live}} Other issues included a perception of rising crime and a lack of parking. The theater's production manager, [[Charles Coles]], said in 1967 that white audiences avoided the Apollo because of the 1964 riots and the rise of race-integrated venues.{{cite news |last=Caldwell |first=Earl |date=November 9, 1967 |title=Fewer Whites Are Taking 'A' Train to Harlem's Night spots; Nightlife Scene Manes in Harlem |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1967/11/09/archives/fewer-whites-are-taking-a-train-to-harlems-night-spots-nightlife.html |access-date=September 7, 2023 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=September 7, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230907211304/https://www.nytimes.com/1967/11/09/archives/fewer-whites-are-taking-a-train-to-harlems-night-spots-nightlife.html |url-status=live}} The Apollo continued to decline through the late 1960s and early 1970s.{{harvnb|Carlin|Conwill|2010|ps=.|p=153}} The Schiffman family was looking to sell the Apollo to black entrepreneurs in the 1960s, having rejected several purchase offers from white theatrical operators. There was also growing support for [[grassroots]] performances at the theater.{{harvnb|Carlin|Conwill|2010|ps=.|pp=178–179}} During that time, the Apollo continued to host variety shows every night and was often sold out during weekends; many of these live acts were accompanied by films.{{cite news |last=Hart |first=Gail |date=September 25, 1973 |title=The Apollo Theatre: A New Look |page=12 |work=Philadelphia Tribune |id={{ProQuest|532631424}}}}{{cite news |last=Campbell |first=Mary |date=September 20, 1970 |title='If You Can Make If at the Apollo...' |page=T1 |work=The Austin Statesman |id={{ProQuest|1635529416}}}} In 1972, a group of investors led by ''New York Amsterdam News'' editor [[Clarence B. The theater had pivoted away from staging comedy and drama and were instead mostly presenting recording groups. Frank Schiffman recalled that the theater's audience at the time was predominantly black and largely consisted of local residents. ==== Decline and closure ==== [[File:Apollo Theatre from west.jpg|alt=The 125th Street facade of the Apollo Theater as seen from the west|thumb|The theater as seen from the west]] Although the Apollo did host some successful shows between 1970 and 1974, the theater's offerings dropped sharply afterward; Herb Boyd wrote in 2009 that "Apollo lovers had to resort to memories rather than performances". By the 1970s, the Apollo was the only remaining black vaudeville theater in the U.S.; other such theaters had closed because they were attracting fewer entertainers and could not compete with large venues. The Apollo Theater was struggling financially by early 1975, forcing its owners to lay off over 100 staff members.{{cite news |last=Stuart |first=Reginald |date=February 16, 1975 |title=Economic Pinch Felt by Small Businesses Here Putting Blacks in Squeeze |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1975/02/16/archives/economic-pinch-felt-by-small-businesses-here-putting-blacks-in.html |access-date=September 18, 2023 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928095842/https://www.nytimes.com/1975/02/16/archives/economic-pinch-felt-by-small-businesses-here-putting-blacks-in.html |url-status=live}} The Apollo had been forced to cut back its schedule of live shows to 20–22 weeks per year, less than half of the 45–50 weeks that the theater had presented in its peak. Management could not raise prices, even by a few cents, because that would drive away the local residents who frequented the theater. In addition, the surrounding area was deserted at night; the Apollo could not afford to pay performers at the significantly higher rates that they demanded; and patrons preferred to watch headliners' performances instead of multi-act shows.{{harvnb|Carlin|Conwill|2010|ps=.|pp=201–202}} To raise money, Robert Schiffman wanted to show [[First run (filmmaking)|first runs]] of films featuring black actors but faced competition from other Manhattan theaters.{{cite news |last=Murray |first=James |date=July 27, 1974 |title=Urban League enters fight on Black film premieres |page=A1 |work=New York Amsterdam News |id={{proQuest|226704104}}}} The Apollo's managers began running for-sale advertisements in several major papers in 1975. The area had also become dangerous; for example, a young patron was killed at the theater later the same year.{{cite news |date=December 7, 1975 |title=Gunman Kills a Man and Shoots Two During Show at the Apollo |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1975/12/07/archives/gunman-kills-a-man-and-shoots-two-during-show-at-the-apollo.html |access-date=September 18, 2023 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928100316/https://www.nytimes.com/1975/12/07/archives/gunman-kills-a-man-and-shoots-two-during-show-at-the-apollo.html |url-status=live}}{{cite news |date=December 8, 1975 |title=Gunman Kills One At Apollo Theater |page=8B |work=The Hartford Courant |issn=1047-4153 |id={{ProQuest|544270933}}}} The Apollo was used exclusively for movies and gospel shows in the mid-1970s{{cite news |last=Patterson |first=Michael |date=September 10, 1976 |title=Harlem nocturne |pages=47 |work=The Reporter Dispatch |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-reporter-dispatch-harlem-nocturne/130821847/ |access-date=September 18, 2023 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928101435/https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-reporter-dispatch-harlem-nocturne/130821847/ |url-status=live}} and was closed in January 1976. The theater had faulty stage equipment and deteriorating facilities, and many of the Apollo's onetime headliners refused to perform there. More obscure acts did not draw large enough crowds to make a profit, and the Apollo had closed by 1977.{{cite news |last=Faller |first=Jan |date=September 23, 1978 |title=Apollo Theatre Alive And Well |page=17 |work=New Pittsburgh Courier |id={{ProQuest|202624095}}}} Robert Schiffman considered replacing the existing theater with a new 3,000-seat venue, and there were also calls to renovate the Apollo or to merge it with the Victoria Theater.{{cite news |last=Poster |first=Thomas |date=January 23, 1978 |title=A Double Play on 2 Great Theaters? |pages=127 |work=New York Daily News |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/daily-news-a-double-play-on-2-great-thea/130824812/ |access-date=September 18, 2023 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928102359/https://www.newspapers.com/article/daily-news-a-double-play-on-2-great-thea/130824812/ |url-status=live}} During the Apollo's closure, the already-dilapidated seats and decorations continued to decay, and burst water pipes destroyed the stage. Robert Schiffman sold the Apollo in early 1978{{cite news |last=Ford |first=Robert Jr. |date=March 25, 1978 |title=Secrecy clouds Apollo's new owners |page=D3 |work=New York Amsterdam News |id={{proQuest|226451523}}}} to a group of black businessmen,{{cite magazine |date=April 8, 1978 |title=General News: MacDonald Will Reopen N.Y.'s Apollo Theatre |magazine=The Billboard |volume=90 |issue=14 |pages=6 |id={{ProQuest|1286321818}}}} who became the first black owners of the theater.{{cite news |last=Palmer |first=Robert |date=May 5, 1978 |title=Lights Go On Again at the Apollo |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1978/05/05/archives/lights-go-on-again-at-the-apollo.html |access-date=September 18, 2023 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928100318/https://www.nytimes.com/1978/05/05/archives/lights-go-on-again-at-the-apollo.html |url-status=live}} The new owners included Rich and Elmer T. Morris and [[Guy Fisher]].{{cite news |last=Branch |first=John |date=November 26, 2010 |title=A Notorious Name, Cast in a New Light |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/11/26/sports/ncaabasketball/26villanova.html |access-date=September 18, 2023 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928102402/https://www.nytimes.com/2010/11/26/sports/ncaabasketball/26villanova.html |url-status=live}} The group spent $250,000 renovating the Apollo,{{cite news |last=Ford |first=Robert Jr. |date=April 1, 1978 |title=Here comes the Apollo – again |page=D12 |work=New York Amsterdam News |id={{proQuest|226404295}}}} which entailed replacing the sound system, renovating backstage areas, and furnishing the lobby. In addition, the new owners hired David E. Apollo's Financing Plan Complete |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1985/01/06/realestate/postings-apollo-s-financing-plan-complete.html |access-date=September 18, 2023 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928101602/https://www.nytimes.com/1985/01/06/realestate/postings-apollo-s-financing-plan-complete.html |url-status=live}}{{cite news |date=November 19, 1984 |title=Apollo Has Guarantee from State |pages=113 |work=New York Daily News |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/daily-news-apollo-has-guarantee-from-sta/130986507/ |access-date=September 18, 2023 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928101136/https://www.newspapers.com/article/daily-news-apollo-has-guarantee-from-sta/130986507/ |url-status=live}} that bank had provided $6 million in total funding.{{cite news |date=May 17, 1985 |title=Rebirth of Harlem's Landmark and a 50-year Heritage |pages=168 |work=New York Daily News |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/daily-news-rebirth-of-harlems-landmark/130987692/ |access-date=September 18, 2023 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928095841/https://www.newspapers.com/article/daily-news-rebirth-of-harlems-landmark/130987692/ |url-status=live}} The first phase cost $5.5 million in total.{{cite magazine |last=Nelson |first=George |date=June 15, 1985 |title=The World of Black Music: Relighting the Apollo at 50: New Luster for Harlem Landmark |magazine=The Billboard |volume=97 |issue=24 |pages=BM6 |id={{ProQuest|1286455098}}}} Local residents hoped that the Apollo's renovation would spur a revival of the neighboring stretch of 125th Street. ==== Reopening and late 1980s ==== The first shows at the refurbished theater were hosted on May 22, 1985.{{cite news |last=Holden |first=Stephen |date=May 22, 1985 |title=The Pop Life; Disco Revival May Be in the Making |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1985/05/22/arts/the-pop-life-disco-revival-may-be-in-the-making.html |access-date=September 18, 2023 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928100554/https://www.nytimes.com/1985/05/22/arts/the-pop-life-disco-revival-may-be-in-the-making.html |url-status=live}} At the time of the rededication, the recording studio was not complete. Sutton had intended to stage a wide variety of genres on different evenings: for example, the Apollo hosted jazz and rock on Friday and Saturday nights, gospel on Sunday mornings, and Amateur Nights on Wednesday nights.{{cite news |last=Davis |first=William A. |date=November 24, 1985 |title=Harlem Bubbles Over With a Restored Sense of Pride |pages=100 |work=The Buffalo News |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-buffalo-news-harlem-bubbles-over-wit/130989261/ |access-date=September 18, 2023 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928102401/https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-buffalo-news-harlem-bubbles-over-wit/130989261/ |url-status=live}} The revived theater also had a mixed-race dance company, which according to Sutton was intended to "send a message that everyone is welcome here". By October 1985, the theater had closed temporarily to accommodate the construction of the recording studio;{{cite news |last=Tapley |first=Mel |date=October 5, 1985 |title=Apollo Theatre re-opening threatened by delays? |page=23 |work=New York Amsterdam News |id={{proQuest|226500033}}}} the ''New York Amsterdam News'' reported two months later that the work would last until late 1986. ''[[Showtime at the Apollo]]'', a TV series showcasing Amateur Night performers, was launched in 1987.{{cite magazine |date=April 8, 1987 |title=Apollo Weekly Television Show Set To Premier This September |magazine=Washington Informer |volume=23 |issue=25 |page=19 |id={{ProQuest|340453141}}}} The facilities were not all complete until mid-1988,{{cite magazine |last=Moss |first=Linda |date=April 11, 1988 |title=Live From the Apollo |magazine=Crain's New York Business |volume=4 |issue=15 |page=1 |id={{ProQuest|219156292}}}} and the renovation ended up costing $20 million.{{cite news |last=Schatz |first=Robin |date=April 21, 1991 |title=Accounting Burlesque at the Apollo Missing files, loose hiring practices cited |page=19 |work=Newsday |issn=2574-5298 |id={{ProQuest|278369524}}}}{{harvnb|Carlin|Conwill|2010|ps=.|p=203}} Sutton's lenders allowed him to defer payments on the loans until 1992 while he tried to make a profit. To raise money, Sutton sold recordings of shows on a [[pay-per-view]] basis and tried to create [[Syndicated television|syndicated TV]] programs at the theater. He also planned to earn money from ''Showtime at the Apollo'', the Apollo Theater Records label, and licensing agreements, but the theater remained unprofitable. Advertising firm [[Saatchi & Saatchi]] signed a contract in 1989 for the exclusive use of the Apollo's broadcast studios,{{cite news |last=Rothenberg |first=Randall |date=April 28, 1989 |title=The Media Business: Advertising; At the Apollo |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1989/04/28/business/the-media-business-advertising-at-the-apollo.html |access-date=September 18, 2023 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928102641/https://www.nytimes.com/1989/04/28/business/the-media-business-advertising-at-the-apollo.html |url-status=live}} but only one syndicated program was created through 1991. The theater was also being used only 50 percent of the time, while the studio's [[uptime]] was 30 percent.{{cite news |last1=Rojas |first1=Don |last2=Boyd |first2=Herb |date=April 13, 1991 |title=Saving the Apollo: Hectic efforts now underway to rescue famous landmark |page=1 |work=New York Amsterdam News |id={{proQuest|226372939}}}} The Apollo was losing $2.4 million a year by 1990{{cite news |date=April 27, 1991 |title=Bank has faith in Apollo Theater |pages=9 |work=The Reporter Dispatch |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-reporter-dispatch-bank-has-faith-in/130588464/ |access-date=September 18, 2023 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928095841/https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-reporter-dispatch-bank-has-faith-in/130588464/ |url-status=live}}{{cite news |last=Schatz |first=Robin |date=April 12, 1991 |title=Apollo Theater Closing Notice Posted |page=7 |work=Newsday |issn=2574-5298 |id={{ProQuest|278356562}}}} and was predicted to lose $2.1 million over the next year. Sutton had expected to earn $1.7 million from videos and pay $1.3 million in salaries in 1990, but he ended up earning $280,000 and paying $1.8 million. The theater still faced competition from larger venues and was affected by perceptions of high crime. The Apollo Theatre Investor Group was delinquent on payments to the UDC by early 1991.{{cite news |last=Schatz |first=Robin |date=April 6, 1991 |title=Apollo Seeks Loan Help Lenders cooperate as payments missed |page=10 |work=Newsday |issn=2574-5298 |id={{ProQuest|278352954}}}} ''Newsday'' reported in 1991 that the group had never kept a formal [[ledger]], which may have worsened its financial issues. Sutton announced in April 1991 that he would shutter the theater on June 1 unless his lenders restructured the loans. After Sutton made a payment of $36,000 later that month, the Manufacturers Hanover Corporation agreed to waive further loan payments for six months.{{cite news |last=Sack |first=Kevin |date=April 27, 1991 |title=Apollo Theater Wins Reprieve on Repayments |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1991/04/27/nyregion/apollo-theater-wins-reprieve-on-repayments.html |access-date=September 18, 2023 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928101306/https://www.nytimes.com/1991/04/27/nyregion/apollo-theater-wins-reprieve-on-repayments.html |url-status=live}} Sutton considered transferring the theater's operation to a new nonprofit organization, which would cost him $6 million. He asked entertainers such as [[Bill Cosby]] to perform at the Apollo to raise money, A network TV special, benefit performances, and film screenings were organized to raise money, and numerous celebrities formed an organization called Save the Apollo Film Committee.{{cite news |last=Farley |first=Christopher John |date=May 6, 1991 |title=Curtain for Apollo?; Debt threatens landmark Harlem theater;Stars rally to save the cultural icon |page=1D |work=USA Today |id={{ProQuest|306429605}}}} Three hundred churches with black congregations also donated to the Apollo,{{cite news |date=August 2, 1991 |title=Black Churches to Aid Hale House, Apollo Theater |pages=34 |work=The Reporter Dispatch |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-reporter-dispatch-black-churches-to/130591105/ |access-date=September 18, 2023 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928101607/https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-reporter-dispatch-black-churches-to/130591105/ |url-status=live}} and State Assembly member [[Geraldine L. Daniels]] asked [[the Recording Academy]] to consider hosting the [[Grammy Awards]] there.{{cite news |date=July 24, 1991 |title=New York Assemblywoman wants Grammy at the Apollo: Daniels calls for awards program in Harlem |page=12 |work=New Journal and Guide |id={{ProQuest|569460465}}}} By July 1991, the Apollo Theatre Investor Group was creating a nonprofit to take over the theater's operation.{{cite news |last=Moore |first=Keith |date=September 27, 1991 |title=Bank Sets New Deal on Apollo |pages=124 |work=New York Daily News |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/daily-news-bank-sets-new-deal-on-apollo/130593168/ |access-date=September 18, 2023 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928102816/https://www.newspapers.com/article/daily-news-bank-sets-new-deal-on-apollo/130593168/ |url-status=live}} === Apollo Theater Foundation operation === In September 1991, the [[New York State Urban Development Corporation]] (UDC) bought the Apollo and assigned its operation to the nonprofit Apollo Theater Foundation (ATF). As part of the deal, Manufacturers Hanover agreed to [[Debt relief|forgive]] $2.9 million in unpaid mortgage payments.{{cite news |date=September 27, 1991 |title=Apollo Goes Nonprofit to Survive |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1991/09/27/nyregion/apollo-goes-nonprofit-to-survive.html |access-date=September 18, 2023 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928095841/https://www.nytimes.com/1991/09/27/nyregion/apollo-goes-nonprofit-to-survive.html |url-status=live}}{{cite news |last=Collins |first=T. J. |date=September 27, 1991 |title=Good News for Apollo |pages=18 |work=Newsday |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/newsday-suffolk-edition-good-news-for/130592963/ |access-date=September 18, 2023 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928101138/https://www.newspapers.com/article/newsday-suffolk-edition-good-news-for/130592963/ |url-status=live}} In addition, the state UDC agreed to restructure a $7.67 million grant, although it was unwilling to forgive the entire debt, which totaled $11.4 million. Performers such as [[Natalie Cole]] continued to host shows to raise money for the Apollo.{{cite news |last=Hinckley |first=David |date=February 19, 1992 |title=Natalie Sings to Save the Apollo |pages=215 |work=New York Daily News |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/daily-news-natalie-sings-to-save-the-apo/130593767/ |access-date=September 18, 2023 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928102359/https://www.newspapers.com/article/daily-news-natalie-sings-to-save-the-apo/130593767/ |url-status=live}} Sutton remained involved with the theater as an unpaid consultant, and Inner City provided $500,000 per year in radio advertising for the Apollo. In addition, Inner City Theater Group licensed the Apollo's name and the rights to use the theater for five years.{{cite news |last1=Finder |first1=Alan |last2=Ramirez |first2=Anthony |date=May 11, 1998 |title=For the Apollo, Audits and Anger; A Landmark, in Eclipse, Faces Questions About Finances |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1998/05/11/nyregion/for-apollo-audits-anger-landmark-eclipse-faces-questions-about-finances.html |access-date=September 8, 2023 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=September 8, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230908001726/https://www.nytimes.com/1998/05/11/nyregion/for-apollo-audits-anger-landmark-eclipse-faces-questions-about-finances.html |url-status=live}} ==== 1990s ==== The ATF took over the theater in September 1992. A plaque, celebrating the Apollo's listing on the [[National Register of Historic Places]], was added to the theater the same month,{{cite news |date=September 9, 1992 |title=Now the Apollo Theater Has a Plaque to Showcase Its Status |pages=46 |work=Chicago Tribune |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/chicago-tribune-now-the-apollo-theater-h/130593394/ |access-date=September 18, 2023 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928101603/https://www.newspapers.com/article/chicago-tribune-now-the-apollo-theater-h/130593394/ |url-status=live}}{{cite news |last1=Poster |first1=Tom |last2=Hester |first2=Jere |date=September 9, 1992 |title=A New Creed for Apollo |pages=584 |work=New York Daily News |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/daily-news-a-new-creed-for-apollo/130593658/ |access-date=September 18, 2023 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928101433/https://www.newspapers.com/article/daily-news-a-new-creed-for-apollo/130593658/ |url-status=live}} although the plaque was stolen in 1996.{{cite news |last=Chetty |first=Sharon |date=April 28, 1996 |title=Neighborhood Report: Harlem; The ATF also created a public museum and held events to pay for maintenance. The revitalization of the Apollo Theater led to increased pedestrian traffic along West 125th Street,{{cite magazine |last=Kamen |first=Robin |date=August 8, 1994 |title=Loans add spice to Harlem eatery |magazine=Crain's New York Business |volume=10 |issue=32 |page=14 |id={{ProQuest|219176294}}}} while the theater itself had 12 events per month, attracting 17,000 guests.{{cite news |last=Lee |first=Felicia R. |date=February 18, 1996 |title=Apollo Mission Woman Aims to Restore Harlem Landmark's Heritage |pages=498 |work=Chicago Tribune |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/chicago-tribune-apollo-mission-woman-aim/130599757/ |access-date=September 18, 2023 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928102816/https://www.newspapers.com/article/chicago-tribune-apollo-mission-woman-aim/130599757/ |url-status=live}} Grace Blake became the ATF's director in 1996. The next year, the Upper Manhattan Empowerment Zone Development Corporation allocated funding for a gift shop next to the theater.{{cite news |date=May 31, 1997 |title=Empowerment Zone unveils $7M in funding recommendations |page=8 |work=New York Amsterdam News |id={{proQuest|390178477}}}} The ATF began raising $30 million for the theater in the late 1990s, but the city and state governments refused to issue $750,000 in grants unless the foundation could provide financial statements.{{cite news |date=May 6, 1998 |title=State, City Officials Block Money for Apollo Theater |pages=21 |work=The Daily Times |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-daily-times-state-city-officials-bl/130604392/ |access-date=September 18, 2023 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928100316/https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-daily-times-state-city-officials-bl/130604392/ |url-status=live}} At the time, there was a dispute over how much Inner City owed the ATF for the use of the Apollo's name.{{cite news |last=Grant |first=Peter |date=June 22, 1998 |title=Impasse on Apollo Could Force 'Showtime' Off Air |pages=53 |work=New York Daily News |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/daily-news-impasse-on-apollo-could-force/130602074/ |access-date=September 18, 2023 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928100545/https://www.newspapers.com/article/daily-news-impasse-on-apollo-could-force/130602074/ |url-status=live}} The Apollo was mostly empty by 1998, except on Amateur Nights, and it was physically deteriorating.{{cite news |last=Span |first=Paula |date=May 28, 1998 |title=Worn Velvet And Fractured Finances At the Apollo; Many black performers shunned the theater because of its small size and because larger venues were no longer segregated. Amateur Night performers came from across the U.S. The vast majority of Amateur Nights performers have historically been young black performers, although there have also been older or white performers. One author wrote in 2010 that "if there had been no Apollo Theater, many of these stars would never have been given their first chance." === Apollo Legends Hall of Fame === The Apollo Legends Hall of Fame was created in 1985. The Hall of Fame initially consisted of the names of 25 performers who debuted at the Apollo before 1955,{{cite news |date=August 1, 1993 |title=This Week's Picks: Historic Apollo Theatre Salutes Its Talent in New Hall of Fame |page=O3 |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 |id={{ProQuest|140825612}}}} as well as memorabilia representing the theater's history. Every year thereafter, up to ten people have been inducted into the Hall of Fame. Nominees for the Hall of Fame are required to have either performed at the Apollo or have created a show or other artistic work inspired by those who performed at the Apollo. Some of the Hall of Fame's inductees are honored in the Walk of Fame, created in 2010. The Apollo Theater (formerly the Hurtig & Seamon's New Theatre; also Apollo Theatre or 125th Street Apollo Theatre) is a multi-use theater at 253 West 125th Street in the Harlem neighborhood of Upper Manhattan in New York City. It is a popular venue for Black American performers and is the home of the TV show Showtime at the Apollo. The theater, which has approximately 1,500 seats across three levels, was designed by George Keister with elements of the neoclassical style. The facade and interior of the theater are New York City designated landmarks and are listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The nonprofit Apollo Theater Foundation (ATF) operates the theater and a recording studio at the Apollo Theater, as well as two smaller auditoriums at the Victoria Theater.
The Apollo was developed by theatrical producers Jules Hurtig and Harry Seamon as a burlesque venue in 1913, and originally served only white patrons. In 1928, the Minsky brothers leased the theater for their own burlesque shows. Sydney Cohen acquired the theater in 1934, and it became a venue for black performers. Frank Schiffman and his family operated the theater from 1935 to 1976. A group of black businessmen briefly operated the theater from 1978 to 1979, and former Manhattan borough president Percy Sutton bought it at an auction in 1981. The Apollo reopened in 1985 following a major refurbishment that saw the construction of new recording studios. In September 1991, the New York State Urban Development Corporation bought the Apollo and assigned its operation to the ATF. Further renovations took place in the mid-2000s, and an expansion of the theater commenced in the 2020s.
Among the theater's longest-running events is Amateur Night at the Apollo, a weekly show where audiences judge the quality of novice performances. Many of the theater's most famous performers are inducted in the Apollo Legends Hall of Fame, and the theater has commissioned various works and hosted educational programs. Over the years, the theater has hosted many musical, dance, theatrical, and comedy acts, with several performers often featured on the same bill. In addition, the theater has hosted film screenings, recordings, and tapings, as well as non-performance events such as speeches, debates, and tributes. The Apollo has had a large impact on African-American culture and has been featured in multiple books and shows.
